title: Metabolic reprogramming of macrophage-specific transketolase orchestrates angiogenesis in diabetic wounds
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 17 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78765-6

Diabetes impairs wound healing by disrupting macrophage metabolism and angiogenesis. Here, authors identify macrophage-specific transketolase (TKT) as a metabolic checkpoint and develop a nanozyme hydrogel that restores macrophage TKT to promote vascular repair in diabetic wounds.
headline: Researchers find a metabolic switch in immune cells that could heal diabetic wounds faster.
why_it_matters: Diabetes makes wounds heal slowly and poorly, often leading to serious complications like amputations. This research identifies a new biological target and a potential treatment that could help millions of diabetic patients recover from injuries more effectively.
key_findings: Transketolase (TKT) — an enzyme that helps cells process sugar — acts as a metabolic checkpoint in macrophages (immune cells that clean up debris and coordinate healing) and is impaired in diabetic wounds.
When TKT function is restored in these immune cells, they switch into a mode that promotes angiogenesis (formation of new blood vessels needed to deliver oxygen and nutrients to healing tissue).
The researchers developed a nanozyme hydrogel (a gel-like material containing tiny engineered particles that mimic enzyme function) that can be applied to wounds to boost TKT activity locally.
This treatment restored blood vessel growth and improved wound healing in a diabetic wound model, suggesting a new therapeutic strategy.
methods_snapshot: The team studied how macrophage metabolism changes in diabetic wounds, identified TKT's role through molecular and cellular experiments, then engineered a nanozyme hydrogel to restore TKT function and tested it on diabetic wound models in the laboratory.

glossary.definition: An enzyme that helps cells break down and recycle sugars to generate building blocks and energy.
A type of white blood cell that cleans up dead cells and debris, and coordinates the body's immune and healing responses.
The biological process of forming new blood vessels.
A shift in how cells process nutrients and generate energy, usually in response to disease or injury.
An engineered nanoparticle (extremely tiny particle) designed to perform chemical reactions like natural enzymes.
A gel-like material that absorbs water and can be applied topically to deliver medicines or therapeutic agents.

limitations: This study was performed in laboratory models of diabetic wounds rather than in human patients, so results may not translate directly to clinical use. The long-term safety and effectiveness of the nanozyme hydrogel in living organisms remain to be tested.
